solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Message from above heralded by 100 saucer-shaped craft? (7)

indicatorNotes.heralded by: a herald goes ahead announcing what follows, so the 100 comes before the message

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
an oracle is a pronouncement from the gods

annotation.surface: A UFO sighting: a flying saucer arrives bearing word from the heavens.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: 'saucer-shaped craft' looks like a flying saucer but is a coracle, a round wicker boat paddled on Welsh rivers.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by shape: the coracle is a small round boat, bowl-like as a saucer.

entries.clue: Detour in force — it’s marked by cones (7)

indicatorNotes.Detour: a detour takes a different route, so the letters of IN FORCE go a different way round

annotation.surface: Roadworks: a diversion is in operation and the route is lined with traffic cones.
annotation.walkthrough: The cones look like the plastic ones of a road diversion; they are pine cones.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by distinguishing feature: bearing cones is what makes a tree a conifer.

entries.clue: One releasing locks to allow access to tower? (8)

annotation.definition: One releasing locks to allow access to tower?

blocks.note: the surface pictures a keyholder undoing door locks; the setter means someone letting down locks of hair
the hair is let down as a ladder so a visitor can climb up into the tower

annotation.surface: A jailer unlocking the doors of a tower.
annotation.walkthrough: In the Grimm fairy tale Rapunzel is shut in a doorless tower and lets down her long hair for the prince to climb.
annotation.definitionFit: A whimsical description of the fairy-tale heroine's defining act.

entries.clue: Unit that is led by mounted police no longer active (5)

indicatorNotes.led by: whatever is led walks behind its leader, so IE comes after the police
indicatorNotes.mounted: something mounted is raised up, and in a down clue that means the letters read upwards

blocks.note: the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police force until 2001

annotation.surface: A mounted police unit that has been disbanded.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mounted police' suggests horses; mounted is the reversal, applied to the RUC, a force that no longer exists.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific example of a unit: the curie is an old measure of radioactivity named after Marie and Pierre Curie.

entries.clue: Broadcast of next episode having turned out so timely (9)

indicatorNotes.Broadcast: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered
indicatorNotes.having turned out: to turn someone out is to evict them, so SO is thrown out of the fodder

blocks.note: S and O are removed, leaving NEXTEPIDE to rearrange

annotation.surface: A trailer for the next episode of a series goes out at just the right moment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'So timely' seems a single phrase; SO belongs to the wordplay and only 'timely' defines.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: what is expedient suits the moment, as a timely act does.

entries.clue: Bowman’s instrument for withdrawing arrows (5)

indicatorNotes.withdrawing: to withdraw is to draw back, so the word is drawn back and runs the other way

blocks.note: a Strad (Stradivarius) is a violin, played by a man with a bow

annotation.surface: An archer's bow, used for pulling arrows back to shoot.
annotation.walkthrough: The bowman seems to be an archer; he is a violinist.
annotation.definitionFit: Pub slang: darts players call their darts arrows.

entries.clue: Party drugs a turn-up for the books? The opposite (3-3)

annotation.definition: a turn-up for the books? The opposite
annotation.surface: A party where drugs turn up is a surprising turn of events.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A turn-up for the books' is British slang for a surprise, which the drugs at the party seem to be; read literally and reversed, it becomes a turn-down in a book.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading of an idiom, inverted: a dog-ear is a page corner turned down in a book.

entries.clue: Take over again on parking in a small spot (7)

indicatorNotes.in: parking in a spot puts the car inside the space, so P goes inside DOT

blocks.note: a dot is a small spot
P = parking, as on road signs

annotation.surface: Someone looking for a tiny parking space.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parking in a small spot' reads as a driver squeezing into a space, which is exactly the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to readopt is to adopt, take over, once more.

entries.clue: Revolutionary is fool to back strike action (3-2)

indicatorNotes.Revolutionary: a revolution is a turn, so IS is turned round
indicatorNotes.to back: backing moves in reverse, so NIT runs backwards

annotation.surface: A radical denounced as an idiot for supporting industrial action.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for an activist; it is an instruction to turn IS round.
annotation.definitionFit: A kind of strike: in a sit-in workers occupy the premises instead of working.

entries.clue: My order turned up around noon from North Africa (8)

indicatorNotes.turned up: turned upside down in a down clue, the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: cor! is a British exclamation like 'my!'
the OM is the Order of Merit
N is the abbreviation for noon

annotation.surface: A diner's meal finally arrives at around twelve, from a North African kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My order' reads as a meal; 'My' is the exclamation and 'order' the honour, together turned upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective by origin: Morocco lies in North Africa.

entries.clue: Admit wrongdoing by publisher binding opponents in contract (3,2)

indicatorNotes.binding: a binding wraps round what it holds, so OUP wraps round WN

blocks.note: in contract bridge, West and North are opponents

annotation.surface: A publishing house confesses to trapping its rivals in a legal agreement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks legal; it is contract bridge, whose players sit at the compass points, so any two neighbours are opponents.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to own up is to confess a fault.

entries.clue: Disgusting ruling backed up boards (9)

indicatorNotes.backed: backed means moved in reverse, so UP runs backwards
indicatorNotes.boards: to board a ship is to get inside it, so PU gets inside REGNANT

annotation.surface: An offensive decision is upheld by the directors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boards' looks like company directors; it is a verb, the reversed UP climbing aboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: repugnant things arouse disgust.

entries.clue: Wrong of church to take possession of flat (7)

indicatorNotes.to take possession of: to possess is to hold, so OF and CE hold FEN between them

annotation.surface: A church seizing someone's apartment is a scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat' reads as an apartment; it is flat wetland, as in the Fens of eastern England.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: an offence is a wrong done, a breach of law or morals.

entries.clue: Battle-axe catching old cavalryman (7)

indicatorNotes.catching: what you catch you hold, so DRAGON holds the O

blocks.note: a battle-axe or dragon is a fierce woman

annotation.surface: A fierce old woman seizes an elderly soldier on horseback.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Battle-axe' looks like a weapon a cavalryman might carry; it is a formidable woman.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind of cavalryman: dragoons were soldiers who rode to battle.

entries.clue: Assortment of bread enclosed in oriental dishes (10)

indicatorNotes.in: enclosed in means held inside, so ENC goes inside CURRIES

blocks.note: enc. = enclosed, as at the foot of a letter

annotation.surface: A selection of breads served alongside curries.
annotation.walkthrough: The breads look like naan and chapati to go with the curries; 'bread' is slang for money.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: bread is money, and an assortment of monies is several currencies.

entries.clue: Lift installed by minder who’s taken over running the estate? (9)

annotation.definition: who’s taken over running the estate?
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a relative clause; read it as 'one who's taken over'

indicatorNotes.installed by: something installed is fitted inside, so the lift goes inside the minder

annotation.surface: A new caretaker has been put in to run a country estate.
annotation.walkthrough: The estate is an estate car (a station wagon), and taking over running it means stealing it.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description by example: a carjacker seizes a car, such as an estate, and drives it.

entries.clue: Winger’s going over for try (4)

indicatorNotes.going over: something going over flips, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a bat is a winger, a winged creature; BAT'S = bat is

annotation.surface: A rugby winger crosses the line to score a try.
annotation.walkthrough: The rugby surface makes 'try' a score; it means an attempt, and the winger is a bat.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: having a stab at something means attempting it.

entries.clue: Attractive person keeping company with maiden (8)

indicatorNotes.keeping: what you keep you hold on to, so BEING holds CO and M

annotation.surface: A charming person who spends time with a young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keeping company with' reads as courting; the phrase splits into the container instruction and the letters it holds.
annotation.definitionFit: An older sense: a becoming dress is one that flatters, making its wearer attractive.

entries.clue: India allowed to detain politician without need for express statement (8)

indicatorNotes.to detain: to detain someone is to hold them, so I and LICIT hold MP between them

blocks.note: I is India in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: India is permitted to hold a politician without charge.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests detention without trial; the definition is the whole last phrase, meaning understood but unsaid.
annotation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: what is implicit is understood without being spelled out.

entries.clue: One of A to G? Yes and no (4)

annotation.definition: One of A to G? Yes and no

blocks.note: the surface reads as a letter of the alphabet; in music the letters A to G name the steps of the scale
the answer both is one of A to G and, split in two, denies being a certain letter among them

annotation.surface: A quiz question answered with a shrug.
annotation.walkthrough: The notes of the scale are named A to G, so 'yes'; but NOTE also splits as NOT E, refusing one of those letters, so 'no'.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by naming convention: musical notes are labelled with the letters A to G.

entries.clue: Senator charged for attempting to overthrow government? (7)

indicatorNotes.charged: charged particles are agitated, so the letters of SENATOR are stirred up

annotation.surface: A senator is indicted for plotting a coup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charged' belongs so naturally to the courtroom story that it hides its job as the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: treason is the crime of betraying or trying to topple one's own state.

entries.clue: Irish, making a comeback in tight match, tie 1-1? (10)

indicatorNotes.making a comeback: coming back means returning the way it came, so IR runs backwards
indicatorNotes.in: in places one thing inside another, so RI goes inside the rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.tight: tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: MATCH TIE rearranged, with RI going in after the A

annotation.surface: An Irish team fights back in a close game to draw one-all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tight match' looks like a close game, and '1-1' like the score; 1-1 is a sum.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one minus one is a small sum, a piece of arithmetic.

entries.clue: Extremists in theory oversaw New York’s oppressive system (7)

indicatorNotes.Extremists in: the extremes of a word are its ends, so take the first and last letters of 'theory'

annotation.surface: Theoretical radicals supervised a harsh New York regime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' reads as radicals; it means the extreme letters of the next word. The 's is 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: tyranny is a system of cruel, absolute rule.

entries.clue: Parisian who cut a piece of cake is feeling sick (6)

indicatorNotes.cut: a cut word is trimmed short, so QUI loses its last letter

blocks.note: qui is French for who; cut, it loses the I
a piece of cake is something easy

annotation.surface: A Frenchman who took a slice of gâteau now feels ill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut a piece of cake' reads as one action; 'cut' works on the French word, and 'a piece of cake' is an idiom.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: queasy describes the nausea of feeling sick.

entries.clue: Mirrors used for inspecting upscale complex (7)

indicatorNotes.complex: complex means intricate, tangled, so the letters of UPSCALE are tangled

annotation.surface: Mirrors fitted for viewings at an upmarket housing development.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complex' looks like a building development; it is the anagram signal. Specula is the Latin plural of speculum.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical term: a speculum is a mirror or medical instrument for examining body cavities.

entries.clue: Part of wicket test umpire checks (5)

indicatorNotes.checks: to check is to hold back, so the phrase holds the answer inside it

annotation.surface: A Test match umpire inspecting the wicket.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket a Test is an international match and the wicket is three upright posts topped by bails, so the surface never leaves the field.
annotation.definitionFit: A part for the whole: a stump is one of the three posts that make a cricket wicket.

entries.clue: Irrational learner driver threatening person on the road to Canterbury? (7)

annotation.definition: person on the road to Canterbury?

blocks.note: British learner drivers display L plates

annotation.surface: A reckless novice at the wheel endangers others on the Canterbury road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' seems to describe the driver; it is a number.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary allusion: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales follows pilgrims travelling to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

entries.clue: Animal expert spending time chasing water bug (5)

indicatorNotes.spending: what you spend is used up and gone, so VET loses its T
indicatorNotes.chasing: a chaser runs behind, so VE comes after PEE

annotation.surface: A zoologist hunts an aquatic insect.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Water bug' reads as an insect; the two words split, water giving letters and bug being the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to bug someone is to irritate them.

entries.clue: Loose articles of French clothing shed (9)

indicatorNotes.clothing: clothing wraps round a body, so UN and LE wrap round SHACK

blocks.note: un and le are French articles

annotation.surface: Baggy French garments being cast off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loose' looks like an adjective for the clothes; it is the verb, as in to loose a prisoner.
annotation.definitionFit: An old verb sense: to loose is to release from bonds.

entries.clue: Clergyman’s piece making a considerable impression in sermon (5)

indicatorNotes.in sermon: a sermon is preached out loud, so the word is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: a cannon is an artillery piece, whose shot makes a big impression

annotation.surface: A cleric's sermon passage has a strong effect on the congregation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a passage of the sermon; it is a gun. The 's is 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific clergyman: a canon is a priest on the staff of a cathedral.

entries.clue: Little finger stained by pen on page (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A on B means A placed after B, so the stained part follows the page

annotation.surface: A writer's small finger smudged by a pen resting on the paper.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures the ink smudge on a writer's hand; the parts come in reverse order, with the page first.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal, chiefly American and Scottish name for the smallest finger.

entries.clue: Frost’s never receding with temperature by turn of year coming back down (2-5)

indicatorNotes.receding: receding means moving back, so NEER runs backwards
indicatorNotes.turn of: a turn spins something round, so YR faces the other way

blocks.note: ne'er, the poetic never a poet such as Robert Frost might use

annotation.surface: Frost never lets up as the temperature falls with the year's turn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frost' seems like weather; it is the American poet Robert Frost, whose 'never' is the poetic contraction.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: re-entry is a spacecraft's return down into the atmosphere.
